absent: No complexity theory, no Juarrero, Levin, Tsing or Santos, and nothing from the Global South or from participatory traditions; constraint is theorised almost entirely through Anglophone psychology and Australian arts education, so power over who sets the constraint never becomes a question.
forYou: 'Active constraints' is the same claim as enabling constraints in your CARN workshop, arrived at from experimental psychology instead of from Juarrero - and the Torrents line on releasing degrees of freedom is close enough to Juarrero's own language to be worth reading as a parallel derivation rather than a competitor.
method: References from Crossref; strands and narrative by Claude, grounded only in the reference list and title.
narrative:
The paper's oldest layer is experimental: Chau (2008), Peterson (2013), Medeiros (2014) and Rietzschel (2014) testing how much limitation a task can carry before creative output falls away, with Haught-Tromp (2017) giving the line its memorable form in the Green Eggs and Ham hypothesis. Tromp's own run of papers (2022, 2023, 2024) then turns that scattered evidence into an integrated model, and it is Tromp's vocabulary of constraint types that the review adopts.

Running alongside it is a quieter and older-feeling lineage from the arts. Kawka (2011) on emergent learning in interactive media, Rowe (2013) on dance as practice research, and Torrents Martin (2015) and Torrents (2021) on constraining movement to release degrees of freedom describe constraint as something that generates form rather than something that limits a subject's output. Richard (2024) carries it forward. These authors sit in a different epistemology from the psychology strand, and the review does not obviously reconcile them.

The third layer is where the argument is actually aimed: assessment. Beck (2013), Harris (2018) on assessment resistance as agency, Villarroel (2018) on authentic assessment, Rickett (2019) on co-constructed rubrics and Wragg (2023) on removing grades treat the assessment regime as the constraint that matters most in teacher education. Underneath all three sits a method apparatus (Arksey, 2005; Tricco, 2018) and a largely Australian arts-teacher-education setting (Davis, 2018; Burke, 2023; Baker, 2026). The unresolved question, carried by Chen (2006), Priest (2006) and Baer (2015), is whether creativity is domain-general enough for any of this to transfer.

strands.name: Constraints as the engine of creativity
strands.note: The tradition the paper grows from: experimental psychology showing that well-placed limits raise rather than depress creative output.

strands.name: Constraint and emergence in movement and the arts
strands.note: A second lineage in which constraints release degrees of freedom and new forms emerge, drawn from dance, media art and motor learning rather than from the lab.

strands.name: Is creativity domain-general?
strands.note: The unresolved argument about whether creativity travels across domains, which decides whether a constraint that works in dance means anything for teacher education.

strands.name: Assessment as the site of the problem
strands.note: Work treating assessment design, rubrics and grading as the thing that makes or breaks creative work, including students' refusal of it.

strands.name: Scoping review method
strands.note: The procedural apparatus the review runs on, from Arksey and O'Malley through PRISMA-ScR to recent critiques of scoping practice.

strands.name: Initial teacher education and the arts
strands.note: The occupational setting: how arts and creativity are taught and assessed in primary and early-childhood teacher preparation, largely Australian.

strands.name: Other / case context
